name: Hypoallergenic bedding / dust mite control

lead: Allergen-proof mattress and pillow covers, hot washing and humidity control cut down dust mite allergens in the bed. Looksmaxxing communities use them to wake with less facial puffiness and less allergic-looking eyes.

House dust mites live in bedding and feed on shed skin, and are a common cause of allergic rhinitis and asthma. Fewer allergens means less allergic reaction overnight and less puffiness in the morning. Avoidance measures are described as reducing mite exposure; no study has tested bedding changes for facial appearance.

paras: Users zip pillows and mattresses into allergen-proof covers, wash sheets in hot water weekly, and keep bedroom humidity low. Partial covers need regular cleaning. Changes are usually judged over a few weeks.
Low risk. The main costs are price and the routine of regular washing.

angle.text: Allergen-proof bedding and hot washing reduce dust mite exposure, which users link to less overnight allergic reaction and a less puffy face and eye area on waking. The approach is established for dust allergy; its effect on facial puffiness has not been studied.

lead: Hypoallergenic bedding and dust mite control means using allergen-proof covers, hot washing and humidity reduction to limit mite allergens, which looksmaxxing communities sometimes link to morning facial puffiness or allergic-looking eyes. House dust mites live in bedding and feed on shed skin, and are a common cause of allergic rhinitis and asthma.[1][2]
Dust mite allergy itself is documented, and avoidance measures are described as reducing exposure; no studies were found testing bedding changes for facial appearance.[2]
infobox: Mite-proof covers, hot washing, low humidity

paras: House dust mites are about 0.2-0.3 mm long and accumulate in mattresses and bedding; surveys have detected mite allergen in about 84% of US beds (2003).[1] Allergy symptoms include sneezing, congestion, and itchy or watery eyes.[2]

Suggested measures include fully enclosing mattress, pillows and duvet in mite-proof covers, weekly bedding changes, hot washing and keeping indoor humidity below about 50%.[1][2] One source notes that attempts to remove mites completely have not been shown to work well.[2]
No studies found on bedding or mite control and facial appearance. Allergen immunotherapy is the main treatment described for mite allergy.[2]
